entries.onMind: the two owl voices on the fourth page
entries.text: Dreamed the net by the door was full of owls instead of acorns, every one of them hooting five times. I tried to count them on one hand and kept running out of fingers.
entries.title: A net of owls

entries.onMind: whether dry ones keep
entries.text: Squeezed the net sack by the herbs. The acorns rattle against each other now instead of thudding, and the one I bit in half was pale and dry right to the middle.
entries.title: Dry all through

entries.text: Ate two handfuls at the table by the lantern. They crunch, and taste more of the fire than of the oak. Through the door the fog lies low between the trunks and I can't see as far as the ring.
entries.title: Breakfast by lantern

entries.onMind: whether the fog is shallower up here than down at the water
queries: why does fog sit low by the creek in the morning
entries.query: why does fog sit low by the creek in the morning
entries.reason: Through the door at breakfast the fog lay low between the trunks and he couldn't see the fire ring.
entries.source: ABC57: Why does fog form near river valleys?
entries.text: The slate says air cools at night, gets heavy and slides down into the lowest ground, and it's there it turns to fog. So the creek is the bottom of everything around here, and the fog collects in it like water in the pool.
entries.title: Cold air goes downhill

entries.text: Nothing in the basket but two leaves, both wet with dew. From the stump the fog looks thinner than at my door, and thicker again down the slope toward the water, the way the slate said.
entries.title: Dew in the basket

entries.onMind: two drawstring cords for the top row of his own net
entries.text: Snapped nettle stalks into the sack at the edge of the brambles. The fog here is only about as deep as the brambles are tall; across the water the tops of the big trunks stand up out of it with no bottoms to them, and nothing else over there shows at all.
entries.title: Trunks with no bottoms

entries.onMind: whether one cord is enough
entries.text: Cracked the nettle stalks on the stump and peeled the long threads off them, then rolled them on my knee into a cord as long as my arm twice. It's greener and scratchier than my last one.
entries.title: Cord off the stalks

entries.onMind: a longer second cord
entries.text: Threaded it through the top row of my net. It goes round once with a hand's length left to knot, and nothing at all left to pull on. I need the second cord after all, and longer.
entries.title: One cord short

entries.onMind: what the far bank looks like with no fog on it
entries.text: Washed the green off my hands at the pool. The fog is lifting off the water in slow rags; the near stepping stones show now, but the far bank is still just gray.
entries.title: Fog coming apart

entries.onMind: how long the dry batch lasts
entries.text: Ate another handful of the dry acorns at my table. The net by the herbs is lighter by about a third now; I should think about what the rest of the week eats.
entries.title: Second breakfast

entries.onMind: whether the rags were where the ground warmed first
queries: why does morning fog lift off water in pieces
entries.query: why does morning fog lift off water in pieces
entries.reason: He watched the fog come apart over the pool in slow rags and wanted to know where it goes.
entries.source: FOX Weather: Does fog really 'burn off'? Dispelling the myth of combustible clouds
entries.text: The slate says the sun doesn't burn fog at all. It warms the ground, the ground warms the air just over it, and the little drops dry up into that air; a breeze stirs in drier air from above too. It never said why it goes in rags, though.
entries.title: Fog doesn't burn

entries.onMind: threading the second cord from the other side
entries.text: Rolled the rest of the nettle on my knee and kept going until the cord reached from my shoulder to my fingertips three times. My knee is green and itchy. This one will go round the top with plenty left to pull.
entries.title: Three arms long

entries.onMind: what the far bank looks like with no fog on it
entries.text: From the table I can see through the door all the way down the slope now, trunk after trunk with their feet showing. The fog has gone back wherever it goes.
entries.title: Clear through the door

entries.onMind: who counts out loud in the forest
entries.text: Pulling the cord through, I heard a voice somewhere down the slope toward the fire ring, low and steady, counting: thirty-nine, forty, forty-one. Then nothing. I leaned to see out the door and there were only trunks.
entries.title: Counting down the slope

entries.text: Threaded the long cord round the top row and knotted the ends together. Pulled, and the whole net gathered up to the size of my fist. My own net is a sack now.
entries.title: It pulls shut

queries: how many acorns can you eat in a day
entries.query: how many acorns can you eat in a day
entries.reason: The net by the herbs is a third lighter already and he wants to know how long the rest lasts.
entries.source: Science Insights: How Many Acorns Do Squirrels Typically Eat in a Day?
entries.text: A squirrel eats ten to twenty acorns a day, about a tenth of its own weight, and twice that before winter. I am a good deal bigger than a squirrel, so I should count on more than twenty.
entries.title: Ten to twenty a day

entries.onMind: a second batch soaking
entries.text: Laid the dry acorns out on the shelf in handfuls of ten. Eleven handfuls. If I eat thirty or forty a day, that is three days, maybe four, and the first batch took two days to soak. I should have started the next one yesterday.
entries.title: Three days of acorns

entries.onMind: sinking the new sack in the creek
entries.text: Gathered acorns under the red oak into the net sack that came in the basket. The wind is out of the west today and smells of salt, and leaves keep coming down through it. Half full already.
entries.title: The new sack fills

entries.reason: The first batch only lasts three or four days, and the creek takes two nights.
entries.text: Cracked the acorns on the stump one at a time under the stone. Forty-six, and seven with grub holes, which I set on the edge of the stump for whoever eats grubs. Thirty-nine good ones in a pale heap.
entries.title: Forty-six cracked

entries.onMind: Who walked past my bench, and why west?
entries.text: Sweeping the shells off the stump, I saw the leaves on the west side of my bench pressed down and scuffed in a line, each scuff longer than my whole foot. The line goes off west toward the lookout. I didn't make it.
entries.title: Scuffed leaves

entries.text: Lifted the flat stone off the old sack at the pool, tipped the thirty-nine meats in from the new net and set the stone back. The water coming off it went brown again straight away. The breeze kept wrinkling the pool so it showed nothing but wrinkles.
entries.title: Back under the stone

entries.onMind: the scuffed line going west
entries.text: Ate a handful from the shelf. Nine handfuls left and a batch in the creek that is ready the day after tomorrow, so it comes out about even if I eat slowly. I kept looking at my own feet and thinking about the scuffs.
entries.title: Two days, then more

entries.onMind: how long the scuffs really are
entries.text: Drew the scuffs on the twenty-third page with the birch pen: a row of long smudges from the bench going west, and my own foot small beside one for size. The ink went on pale; it will darken.
entries.title: The line on paper

entries.onMind: whether a long foot means a tall someone
entries.text: Set my foot in one of the scuffs. It takes two of my feet to fill it, and the next one is farther off than two of my strides. The leaves are smeared, not printed; no toes, no edges, nothing I could draw round.
entries.title: Two of my feet

entries.onMind: where the line goes past the boulder
queries: how tall is someone from the size of their footprint
entries.query: how tall is someone from the size of their footprint
entries.reason: The scuffs by his bench take two of his feet to fill, and he wanted to know what that says about whoever made them.
entries.source: Giles and Vallandigham 1991: Height Estimation from Foot and Shoeprint Length
entries.text: The slate says a foot is about a seventh of how tall someone is, but a print made with something on the feet comes out longer than the foot inside it. These are smears in leaves, not prints, so I can't tell a big foot from a big shoe from a slide. Whoever it is might be tall, or might not.
entries.title: A foot and a seventh

entries.onMind: Whoever went out to the edge has to come back this way.
entries.text: The scuffs go round the foot of the mossy boulder and straight on west, toward the edge where I watch the sun go down. The wind has turned and comes from the north now, with no salt in it. I didn't follow.
entries.title: Past the boulder

entries.text: Ate a handful of the dry acorns at my table. Eight handfuls left on the shelf. My legs feel the walk to the boulder and back more than they should.
entries.title: Eight handfuls now

entries.onMind: someone who counts their steps
entries.text: The counting came again, from up the slope by my bench this time: seventy-nine, eighty, eighty-one, eighty-two, eighty-three. Then it stopped. The same low, steady voice as this morning.
entries.title: Counting again

entries.text: Wrote both counts on the twenty-fourth page: forty-one this morning down by the ring, eighty-three now up by my bench. Whoever it is counts their steps, the way I count breaths for a leaf on the creek.
entries.title: Two counts

entries.text: A second line of scuffs lies over the first by my bench, fresher, with the damp undersides of the leaves turned up. One line went out west and one came back, and they cross right beside the stump. From the scuffs alone I can't tell which is which.
entries.title: A line coming back

queries: how to tell which way someone walked through dry leaves
entries.query: how to tell which way someone walked through dry leaves
entries.reason: He wants to know which way the walker went last.
entries.source: To Know the Land: Determining Direction of Travel on a Fisher Trail
entries.text: The slate says whatever a foot kicks up lands mostly at the front of the track, where the foot lifts out, so the heap points the way someone went. A hard push-off can throw some backward too, so it says to check more than one sign.
entries.title: Leaves pile up in front

entries.onMind: the scuffs heading east toward the creek
entries.text: Looked down at the fresh scuffs again. The loose leaves are heaped at the east end of every one. Whoever went out to the edge has come back past my bench and gone on toward the fire ring and the water.
entries.title: Went toward the water

entries.onMind: the print by the ring
entries.text: Where I swept the ground bare around the ring, one whole print is pressed into the dirt, longer than two of my feet. It has straight lines across the front and a square heel set apart from the rest, as if the foot stood on a little block. Something was on that foot.
entries.title: A print in the bare

entries.onMind: the scuffs running to the stepping stones
entries.text: Past the edge of the bare circle the scuffs start again in the leaves and run east, toward the stepping stones. I stayed at the ring.
entries.title: On toward the stones

entries.onMind: nicks in the lines
queries: footprint in dirt with lines across the bottom and a separate square heel what made it
entries.query: footprint in dirt with lines across the bottom and a separate square heel what made it
entries.reason: He wanted to know what kind of foot leaves straight lines and a square heel.
entries.source: Off Grid Web: Footprint Analysis 101: Getting a Foot Message
entries.text: The slate says the heel is usually the deepest, clearest part of a print because it comes down first and hardest. The lines are the pattern of whatever is worn on the foot, and each one collects its own nicks and cuts over time, so a print can tell one walker from another.
entries.title: The heel tells most

entries.onMind: the bite in the third line
entries.text: Looked again. The heel is pressed in deepest, like the slate said, and the third line from the front has a small bite out of it. If I ever see that bite again, I will know it is the same foot.
entries.title: A bite out of a line

entries.onMind: whoever wears a foot like that
entries.text: Drew the print on the twenty-fifth page with the lines, the square heel and the bite, and my own foot beside it twice over for size. The leaves are already blowing back onto the bare circle in this little breeze.
entries.title: Twenty-fifth page

entries.onMind: where the toes point
entries.text: Followed the scuffs down to the first stepping stone. In the soft mud beside it is the same print, the same small bite out of the third line, and its toes point straight at the water.
entries.title: The same bite

entries.onMind: two round shining things
entries.text: From the first stone the far bank was plain in the sun: the gray-blue shape hung between two poles, and under it someone bent over a table of planks, with hair standing up in points. Two round things on its face caught the sun once. Then a small tap, like something set down, and only the creek.
entries.title: Under the gray shape

entries.reason: The stones were right there, but nothing in his own day needed the other side.
entries.text: I didn't cross. Whoever it is was busy with their hands, the way I am at my bench, and I wouldn't want someone walking up the slope at me in the middle of a knot.
entries.title: Not my side

entries.text: Ate a handful of the dry acorns at my table. Seven handfuls left on the shelf. My legs stopped buzzing about halfway through.
entries.title: Seven handfuls

entries.onMind: goggles
queries: what are the round glass things some people wear over their eyes
entries.query: what are the round glass things some people wear over their eyes
entries.reason: The figure across the water had two round things on its face that caught the sun.
entries.text: The slate says round glass worn in front of the eyes is called glasses, and people wear them to see better, to keep bright sun out, or to keep flying bits out of their eyes. The sturdy kind for flying bits are called goggles. Over there they tink and rasp and grind all day; bits must fly.
entries.title: Glass in front of eyes

entries.text: Drew it on the twenty-sixth page: the gray shape on two poles, the plank table, a bent back, hair in points, and two small circles where the eyes go. I wrote goggles beside the circles with a question mark.
entries.title: Twenty-sixth page

entries.onMind: something besides acorns
entries.text: The small gray oyster mushrooms I left on the fallen oak are as wide as my palm now. Cut four into the sack and left the smallest ones again.
entries.title: Wide as my palm

entries.onMind: coals for the mushrooms
entries.text: Lit the fire in the ring, the first one today. The ground is dry and the smoke leaned off north in the light breeze.
entries.title: First fire today

entries.text: Ate the mushrooms hot off a stick on the log seat, a little chewy and nothing like acorns. The seven handfuls stay on the shelf tonight.
entries.title: Not acorns

entries.onMind: the one in goggles
entries.text: From the log seat the trunks hide the stepping stones. If the one in goggles looks this way, all they will see is my smoke.
entries.title: Only smoke

queries: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow on a log
entries.query: how fast do oyster mushrooms grow on a log
entries.reason: The small ones he left on the fallen oak were as wide as his palm by evening.
entries.source: Field & Forest Products: Oysters Mushrooms on Logs
entries.text: The slate says oyster mushrooms come up suddenly and grow quickly once they start, mostly in fall and most of all after a heavy rain, so you should check the log often. Pick them while the edges of the caps are still curled down. It never said how many days.
entries.title: They come up fast

entries.onMind: the small mushrooms on the fallen oak
entries.text: Wrote the fallen oak on the twenty-seventh page: four cut tonight, the small ones left, and 'pick while the edges curl under'. The ones I ate tonight had flat edges. I'll look at the oak every morning now.
entries.title: Twenty-seventh page

entries.onMind: what knocked at the stump
entries.text: One knock of metal on wood from up the slope toward the stump, loud in the quiet, and then nothing. No counting this time. I kept the pen on the page and didn't go up.
entries.title: A knock up the slope

entries.text: Fed four sticks onto the fire. It caught up high and the sparks went straight up; the breeze has gone soft and comes from the south now.
entries.title: Sticks on

entries.onMind: the knock at the stump
entries.text: The light between the trunks to the west went orange and then gray. Past my bench the sun is going into the water at the edge, and tonight I stayed with the fire instead. In the morning I'll look in the basket first.
entries.title: Going into the water

entries.onMind: a pen that doesn't go blunt
entries.text: Started a new birch pen on the log seat while the fire is high. Shaved the end to a slant, slow, so the split runs straight.
entries.title: A spare pen

entries.onMind: who walks round a fire instead of up to it
entries.text: Steps in the dry leaves off past the scarred trunk, quick, going east toward the creek, and one small clink. Past the firelight it was too dark to see anything. They went the long way round my fire, the same as the knock did.
entries.title: Steps to the north

entries.onMind: the curve around the fire
entries.text: Wrote the steps on the twenty-eighth page: north of the fire, going east, one clink, just as the light went. Drew an arrow for which way, and a little fire with a wide curve around it.
entries.title: Twenty-eighth page

entries.onMind: letting the fire burn down
queries: how far away can you see a campfire at night in the woods
entries.query: how far away can you see a campfire at night in the woods
entries.reason: Someone keeps going round his fire in the dark, and he wanted to know how far off it can be seen.
entries.source: Preparedness Advice: How Far Away Can You See a Candle at Night?
entries.text: The slate says on a dark night even a candle can be seen miles off over open ground, and that the lay of the land is what hides a light. It said nothing about trees, but here the trunks are my land.
entries.title: How far a fire shows

entries.onMind: the one in goggles
entries.text: Whoever it is already knows where my fire is; they walk round it. I won't feed it again tonight and let it go down to coals on its own.
entries.title: No more sticks

entries.onMind: the wind from the north
entries.text: The wind swung round to come from the north and started flicking sparks past the swept circle into the dry leaves. I scraped ash over the coals with a stick and pushed the ring stones in until nothing showed orange.
entries.title: Banked it after all

entries.text: Ate a handful of soaked acorns at my table with the door shut against the wind. Six handfuls left on the shelf.
entries.title: Supper at the table

entries.onMind: a colder morning
queries: why does the wind turn around and come from the north in the evening and get colder
entries.query: why does the wind turn around and come from the north in the evening and get colder
entries.reason: All day the breeze came soft from the south, and at dark it swung round from the north and felt drier.
entries.source: theweatherprediction.com: Wind Direction and Weather Forecasting
entries.text: The slate says a south wind usually brings warmer air and a north wind cooler, drier air, and a sudden swing from one to the other can mean a whole new air is coming through. So the warm days may be over for a while.
entries.title: Wind from the north

entries.onMind: dry sticks for the morning fire
entries.text: If colder air is coming in on this wind, the morning fire will be slow to catch. Before bed I'll carry an armful of dry sticks inside the door so they don't take the dew.
entries.title: Dry sticks by the door

entries.onMind: a fire that catches on the first try
entries.text: Pulled dry sticks out from under the leaf heap past the log seat. The top leaves were damp, but the sticks under them snapped clean. Carried an armful home and stood it inside the door.
entries.title: Sticks from the heap

entries.onMind: what slides over there
entries.text: With my arms full, a thin flat clatter came across the water, like the sheets sliding again. The yellow light sat steady in its low spot, and the north wind took the rest of the sound away south.
entries.title: A clatter across

entries.onMind: the knobs on the fallen oak
queries: do oyster mushrooms keep growing when it gets cold
entries.query: do oyster mushrooms keep growing when it gets cold
entries.reason: The slate said colder air is coming on the north wind, and the small caps on the fallen oak are what he eats when the acorns run short.
entries.source: Permies: Can oyster mushrooms be grown in cold temperatures?
entries.text: People there grow oysters at about fifty degrees, some kinds a little colder, but say they stop outdoors in real winter. Nobody said how much slower they get. If this cold is only a little cold, the knobs on the oak should still come on.
entries.title: Mushrooms in the cold

entries.text: Whittled the spare pen's tip at my table and cut the slit back to a grain of rice. No ink in here; it stays in the stone by the fire. In the morning it goes on the middle shelf with the other two.
entries.title: The spare pen

entries.onMind: the knobs on the fallen oak
entries.text: The wind leans on the door and finds the gap at the bottom. First thing tomorrow I look at the oak, then the basket.
entries.title: Wind under the door

entries.reason: With no wind to throw sparks, he wanted the ink warm to try the new pen.
entries.text: Opened the door and the north wind had dropped to almost nothing; the leaves on the slope lay still. Took half the sticks from inside the door down to the ring and lit a small fire on the first breath.
entries.title: Wind gone quiet

entries.text: Small quick taps came across the water, metal on metal, a long row of them, then they stopped. The yellow light sat in its low spot the whole time.
entries.title: Tapping across

entries.text: Dipped the spare pen for the first time. It holds ink for most of a line and the slit didn't spread. Wrote the north wind and how it went quiet on the twenty-ninth page.
entries.title: Third pen

entries.onMind: the wind coming back down at sunup
queries: why does the wind die down at night
entries.query: why does the wind die down at night
entries.reason: The north wind he expected to blow cold all night went quiet within an hour.
entries.source: The Weather Guys: Why does the wind diminish after sunset?
entries.text: The slate says after sundown the ground cools faster than the air over it, so the low air goes cold and heavy and stops mixing with the faster wind higher up. The wind is still blowing up there; it just can't reach the leaves until the sun warms the ground again.
entries.title: Where the wind went

entries.text: Ate the handful of soaked acorns I carried down in the bindle, on the log seat. Five handfuls left on the shelf.
entries.title: Five handfuls

entries.onMind: the oak first thing, then the basket
entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals and pushed the ring stones in. If the wind comes back down when the sun warms the ground, the way the slate says, it will find nothing here to throw.
entries.title: Banked tight

queries: how to keep homemade acorn ink from drying out overnight
entries.query: how to keep homemade acorn ink from drying out overnight
entries.reason: The ink in the stone by the fire grew a skin and went thick as mud once before, and tonight it sits open again.
entries.source: The Graphics Fairy: How to Make Acorn Ink
entries.text: The page says to keep ink in a jar with a tight lid, somewhere cool, and that ink left in an open dish overnight loses its water and goes darker and thicker. Mine lives in a hollow in a stone with no lid at all.
entries.title: Ink in the open

entries.onMind: a bark lid for the ink stone
entries.text: I don't have a jar, but I have plenty of birch. In the morning I cut a square of bark to lay over the hollow and put a pebble on it.
entries.title: A lid for the stone

entries.text: Sorted the soaked acorns on the shelf into two handfuls for breakfast and three for later. Fresh ones go in the creek tomorrow so something is soaking behind these.
entries.title: Breakfast set aside
